## About this lecture

Your data almost never arrive as one flat list of independent numbers. They come **grouped**: several cells per animal, several reads per cell, several time points per patient. Today we learn to model that structure instead of pretending it isn't there.

- **Biological vs technical replicates** — and why confusing them (**pseudoreplication**) is one of the most common mistakes in the literature.
- **Three ways to handle grouped data**: pool everything, pool nothing, or the middle road — **partial pooling**.
- **Shrinkage**: group estimates are pulled toward the overall mean, more so when a group is small or noisy.
- **Random effects**: a patient level and a measurement level; the same idea in `lme4` and Bayesian `brms`/Stan syntax.
- Why hierarchy gives you the **right uncertainty**, not just the right average.

::: notes
The one sentence to leave the room with: measurements taken on the same biological unit are not independent, and a model that ignores that will report false confidence. Everything else today — replicates, pooling, shrinkage, random effects — is machinery for respecting that grouping. This builds directly on the Bayesian ideas of prior, likelihood and posterior: a hierarchical model is, in effect, a model that learns its own prior for the group-level parameters from the data.
:::

## A biology picture first {.smaller}

You measure a blood biomarker to compare **treated vs control** patients. But you don't get one number per patient — you draw **several samples per patient**, and each sample is assayed.

- 6 patients, roughly 5 measurements each → about 30 numbers.
- The 5 measurements from one patient are **more similar to each other** than to another patient's: same physiology, same day, same tube.

**How many independent data points do you really have — 30, or 6?**

The honest answer is *somewhere between*, and today's model is exactly what puts a number on "somewhere between".

![](fig02-patient-clusters.svg){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: notes
Anchor everything in this concrete design before any equation. The tension is entirely captured by the question "30 or 6?". Naively treating all 30 as independent (this is pseudoreplication) exaggerates your sample size and shrinks your p-values dishonestly. Treating each patient as a single averaged number throws away the within-patient information and the fact that some patients were measured more than others. The hierarchical model keeps all 30 numbers but counts them correctly. Keep the biomarker example running through the whole lecture.
:::

## The replicate question {.smaller}

Before any statistics, ask of every number: **what is being repeated?**

- **Biological replicate** — an independent biological unit: a different patient, animal, or independently grown culture. Captures **biological variation** between units.
- **Technical replicate** — the same biological unit measured again: the same blood sample split and assayed twice, the same library sequenced twice. Captures **measurement / assay noise** only.

Averaging two technical replicates makes your *measurement* of one unit more precise. It does **not** give you a second unit.

::: {.callout-note}
The number that limits your ability to **generalise** to new patients is the number of **biological** replicates, not the total count of measurements.
:::

![](fig03-bio-vs-tech-replicate.svg){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: notes
This distinction is the conceptual core and where most real errors live. Technical replicates reduce measurement error about a single unit; biological replicates are what let you say anything about the population. A study with 3 mice measured 100 times each has n = 3 for the biological question, not 300. Students with a wet-lab background usually recognise this immediately from grant/reviewer feedback; students from a pure data background often have not internalised it. Tie it to the earlier Poisson / negative binomial idea that different sources of variation stack.
:::

## Pseudoreplication {.smaller}

**Pseudoreplication** = analysing technical replicates (or repeated measures within a unit) as if they were independent biological replicates.

Consequences:

- The **effective sample size** is overstated (you claim 30 when you have nearer 6).
- Standard errors come out **too small**, confidence intervals **too narrow**.
- p-values are **too optimistic** → inflated false-positive rate.

A classic tell in a paper: "n = 240 cells from 3 animals, p < 0.001." The relevant *n* for a between-animal claim is **3**.

![](fig04-ci-narrow-vs-wide.svg){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: notes
Give the name and make it stick — pseudoreplication (Hurlbert's term) is a citable, recognised problem, not a nitpick. The mechanism is simply that within-unit measurements are positively correlated, so each additional one carries less than a full data point's worth of new information; standard formulas that assume independence divide by too large an n. The "240 cells from 3 animals" pattern is worth having them memorise as a red flag they will genuinely see in seminars. The fix is not to throw data away but to model the grouping, which is the rest of the lecture. The "counting cells vs counting patients" demo after the ICC slide shows how large the damage is: 41% false positives instead of 5% at modest clustering.
:::

## Three ways to handle grouped data {.smaller}

Say each patient has their own true mean and you want to estimate it.

1. **Complete pooling** — ignore patients; one grand mean $\mu$ for everyone. *Throws away real between-patient variation.*
2. **No pooling** — a separate, independent mean for each patient, estimated from that patient's data alone. *Noisy for patients with few measurements; can't borrow strength.*
3. **Partial pooling** — each patient's estimate is a **compromise** between the patient's own mean and the grand mean. *The hierarchical model.*

Partial pooling is the "have your cake and eat it": patient-specific, but stabilised by the group.

![](fig05-three-pooling.svg){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: notes
Frame these as the two extremes and the middle. Complete pooling assumes all patients are identical (between-patient variance = 0). No pooling assumes patients tell you nothing about each other (between-patient variance = infinity). Neither is usually true. Partial pooling estimates *how* similar patients are from the data and lets that estimate set the compromise. Emphasise "borrow strength": a patient with only two noisy measurements gets rescued toward the group, while a patient with twenty measurements barely moves.
:::

## Partial pooling and shrinkage {.smaller}

The partial-pooling estimate for a patient is a **weighted average** of its own mean and the grand mean:

$$
\text{estimate} \;=\; w \cdot \text{own mean} \;+\; (1-w) \cdot \text{grand mean}
$$

The weight $w$ (between 0 and 1) says **how much the patient's own data is worth compared with the crowd**:

$$
w \;=\; \frac{n/\sigma^2}{\,n/\sigma^2 + 1/\tau^2\,}
$$

- $n/\sigma^2$ — worth of the patient's own data: more measurements ($n$), less noise ($\sigma^2$) → worth more.
- $1/\tau^2$ — worth of the crowd: the more alike patients are (small spread $\tau^2$) → worth more.

Example: $n = 4$, $\sigma^2 = 8$, $\tau^2 = 2$ gives $w = 0.5/(0.5+0.5) = 0.5$; own mean 10, grand mean 6 → estimate 8.

The pull toward the grand mean is **shrinkage**: strongest when a patient has **few** measurements or patients are **truly alike** ($\tau^2$ small).

![](fig06-precision-weight-balance.svg){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: notes
The weighted average carries the whole idea; read the weight as plain arithmetic, no derivation needed. The patient's own data are worth more with more measurements and less noise (n / sigma^2); the crowd is worth more when patients are alike (1 / tau^2, large when tau^2 is small). w is the patient's share of the total worth. A data-rich patient leans on itself; a data-poor patient leans on the crowd. Work the example aloud: both worths are 0.5, so w = 0.5 and the estimate sits halfway between 10 and 6, at 8 (exercise B3). The two extremes from the previous slide come back in the demo two slides on: drag tau^2 to 0 and everyone collapses onto the grand mean (complete pooling); drag it to infinity and everyone keeps their own mean (no pooling). Shrinkage is not a fudge — it is the estimate that minimises expected error when groups genuinely share a distribution, echoing the Bayesian posterior-mean idea from earlier in this block.
:::

## Shrinkage, drawn {.smaller}

![](fig07-shrinkage-dumbbell.svg){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

Picture each patient's raw mean on the left and its shrunken estimate on the right:

- Points **move toward the grand mean**, never past it.
- Patients with **few / noisy** measurements move the **most**.
- Patients with **many** measurements barely move — they've earned their position.

This is *regularisation*: extreme group estimates, which are often extreme only by chance, are reined in. `lfcShrink` in *Bulk RNA-seq with DESeq2* did the same to fold changes: low-count genes moved most towards 0.

::: notes
The dumbbell / caterpillar picture is the single most memorable image for shrinkage; describe it even without the figure. The key intuition to install: an extreme raw group mean is more likely to be extreme because of sampling noise than because the group is genuinely extreme, so pulling it toward the centre improves it on average. This is the same logic as ridge/penalised regression coming later in Penalized linear models, and the same logic as a Bayesian prior: both discipline extreme estimates. The lfcShrink recall: genes play the role of patients, a gene's read count the role of the number of measurements, and the centre is a fold change of 0. Note the "never past the grand mean" property — shrinkage interpolates, it doesn't overshoot.
:::

## Try it: how much to shrink {.smaller}

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="shrinkage" data-n="1 2 2 3 5 8 12 20" data-mu="6" data-sigma2="8" data-tau2="2" data-xlabel="biomarker (patient mean)"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/shrinkage.js"></script>
```

::: notes
Eight simulated patients with between 1 and 20 measurements each, using the numbers from the exercise: within-patient variance sigma^2 = 8, true between-patient variance tau^2 = 2, overall mean 6. Open dots are the raw patient means, filled dots the partially pooled estimates, the green tick is the true patient mean (we only know it because we simulated it), and the weight w is printed on the right. Start at the true tau^2 and point at the n = 1 patient: w = 0.2, it moves most; the n = 20 patients barely move. Drag tau^2 down to 0: every filled dot collapses onto the grand mean (complete pooling). Drag it to infinity: filled dots sit on the open dots (no pooling). Then read the error box and the red curve: total squared error against the truth is usually lowest somewhere in between — that is the payoff of shrinkage. Press "new data" a few times to show this holds on most, not all, data sets, and that individual patients can get worse while the total improves.
:::

## Random effects: the two-level model {.smaller}

Each measurement = **overall mean** + **patient level** + **measurement level**:

- **Overall mean** — one number for everyone (a **fixed effect**).
- **Patient level** — how far this patient sits from the overall mean (a **random effect**). Patients scatter with spread $\tau$ (*between* patients).
- **Measurement level** — noise around the patient's own value, with spread $\sigma$ (*within* a patient).

The move that makes it *hierarchical*: the patient offsets are not free numbers — they come from **one shared spread** $\tau$, which is **estimated from the data**.

![](fig08-two-level-random-effects.svg){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: notes
Two levels, two spreads: sigma lives between measurements of one patient (technical), tau lives between patients (biological). This is exactly the biological/technical distinction from earlier, now as a model. Walk the figure: overall mean, each patient's offset, then the measurements scattered around each patient. The crucial and initially strange idea is that the patient offsets are treated as draws from one shared distribution rather than as ordinary parameters we estimate freely — that shared distribution is what couples the patients together and produces partial pooling automatically. Because tau is learned from the data, the model discovers how much to pool. Contrast "fixed effect" (one number for the whole dataset) with "random effect" (one draw per group from a common pool). The equation version is on the optional slide at the end.
:::

## The variance partition (ICC) {.smaller}

The two variances answer "how correlated are two measurements from the *same* patient?"

$$
\text{ICC} \;=\; \frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2 + \sigma^2}
$$

- **ICC near 1** — patients differ a lot, measurements within a patient are tight. Grouping matters enormously; your effective sample size is close to the **number of patients**.
- **ICC near 0** — patients are basically interchangeable; grouping barely matters and complete pooling is nearly fine.

The **intraclass correlation** is the single number that tells you *how much* your hierarchy matters.

![](fig09-icc-variance-bars.svg){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: notes
ICC = fraction of total variance that is between-group. It is the same quantity that governs how much pseudoreplication would have hurt you: high ICC means within-group measurements are highly redundant, so counting them all as independent is very wrong. Give the two poles. A useful mental check: with high ICC, going from 5 to 50 measurements per patient barely helps the between-patient question — you need more patients. This directly answers the opening "30 or 6?" question quantitatively.
:::

## Try it: counting cells vs counting patients {.smaller}

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="pseudorep" data-icc="0.2" data-patients="3" data-cells="20"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/pseudorep.js"></script>
```

1000 simulated studies where treatment does nothing: how often does each analysis cry "significant"?

::: notes
This replaces the error-bar argument with a simulation, and it is the pseudoreplication slide brought to life. Each simulated study has 3 control and 3 treated patients, 20 cells each, and no true difference. The top picture is one study: dots are cells, one colour per patient, with patient averages and group averages. The bars count, over 1000 such studies, how often each analysis gives p < 0.05. "Every cell as a sample" treats all 120 cells as independent (pseudoreplication); "average per patient first" uses one number per patient, which is about what the mixed model does. At the defaults (ICC 0.2): the naive analysis calls 41% of the null studies significant, the per-patient analysis 6.0%, close to the honest 5% (dashed line). The readout says 120 cells are worth about 25 effective samples, not 120. Drag ICC to 0.3 and cells per patient to 50: naive false alarms rise to 65%, and the effective samples fall to about 19 even though there are more cells. More cells per patient makes the naive analysis worse, not better. Drag ICC to 0: now both are fine, because the cells really are independent. The message: the hierarchical model gives the same data honest error bars, tied to the number of patients, not the number of measurements. Exercise E5 uses the fixed-budget switch to compare designs.
:::

## In R: the model formula {.smaller}

The grouping is written with `(1 | patient)` — read it as "let the intercept vary by patient."

Frequentist multilevel fit with `lme4`:

```r
library(lme4)

# random intercept per patient, plus a treatment fixed effect
set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(patient = factor(rep(seq_len(40), each = 4)),
                treatment = rep(c("control", "control", "treated", "treated"), 40))
patient_effect <- rnorm(40, sd = sqrt(2))
d$biomarker <- 6 + 1.5 * (d$treatment == "treated") +
  patient_effect[as.integer(d$patient)] + rnorm(nrow(d), sd = sqrt(8))
fit <- lmer(biomarker ~ treatment + (1 | patient), data = d)

summary(fit)     # fixed effects + variance of the random intercept (tau^2) and residual (sigma^2)
ranef(fit)       # the shrunken per-patient offsets
```

- `treatment` — a **fixed** effect (the population-level question).
- `(1 | patient)` — a **random** intercept: one offset per patient, all from one shared spread $\tau$.

::: notes
Keep this static — nothing is installed at render time — and read the formula syntax aloud because it is the part students actually reuse. Everything left of the bar is what varies by group (here just 1, the intercept); everything right of the bar is the grouping factor. summary() reports the two variance components, which are tau^2 and sigma^2 from the two-level picture, plus the fixed-effect estimate and its (correctly widened) standard error. ranef() returns the partially pooled patient offsets — those are the shrunken estimates from the dumbbell picture. lme4 is the standard non-Bayesian entry point; the next slide gives the Bayesian version.
:::

## The Bayesian version: brms / Stan {.smaller}

The **same formula**, now fully Bayesian — priors on every parameter, a posterior for each:

```r
library(brms)

fit <- brm(biomarker ~ treatment + (1 | patient),
           data = d,
           family = gaussian())      # brms writes and runs the Stan model for you

summary(fit)                          # posterior means + credible intervals
```

The hierarchy is Bayesian at heart: "patient offsets scatter with spread $\tau$" **is** a prior on the patient offsets. It is an **adaptive prior**: its width $\tau$ is not fixed in advance but learned from the data, and $\tau$ gets a (vaguer) prior of its own, a *hyperprior*.

::: notes
The punchline that ties the block together: a random effect is literally a prior on the group-level parameters, and because tau is learned, it is an *adaptive* or *hierarchical* prior — the data tell you how strongly to pool. This is why hierarchical models feel so natural in the Bayesian framework and why brms uses the identical (1 | patient) syntax on top of Stan. Everything from the prior/likelihood/posterior lectures applies unchanged; we've just added a layer where a parameter's prior has parameters of its own. Don't dwell on MCMC mechanics here — the point is conceptual continuity, not sampler details.
:::

## Reading it off correctly {.smaller}

Whichever engine you use, the workflow is the same:

- Report the **fixed effect** (e.g. treatment difference) with its interval — this is your scientific answer.
- Report the **variance components**: $\hat\tau$ (between patients) and $\hat\sigma$ (within patients); their ratio gives the ICC.
- Use the **shrunken** per-group estimates (`ranef` / posterior) when you need patient-level values, never the raw per-patient means.

A one-line sanity check: if $\hat\tau \approx 0$ the data say patients are alike (near complete pooling); if $\hat\tau \gg \hat\sigma$ grouping dominates.

::: notes
Give them a concrete reporting checklist so the model output isn't opaque. The fixed effect answers the biology; the variance components describe the structure and let a reader compute the ICC and judge how much pooling happened. Warn them not to grab raw group means after fitting a hierarchical model — the whole point was to improve those via shrinkage. The tau-hat sanity check connects the fitted numbers back to the three-ways slide: the model chose its own spot on the pooling spectrum, and tau-hat tells you where.
:::

## Pitfalls and good practice {.smaller}

- **Too few groups.** You cannot estimate $\tau$ from 2–3 patients; the between-group variance is barely identified. Rule of thumb: aim for **more groups**, not just more measurements per group.
- **Crossed vs nested grouping.** Cells within patients within hospitals *nest*; but batch and patient may *cross*. Write the grouping to match the design.
- **Don't model the treatment as random** if it's the effect you care about and has few, deliberately chosen levels — that's a fixed effect.
- **Balance isn't required.** Unequal numbers of measurements per patient are fine and handled automatically — that's a strength over averaging.

![](fig14-nested-vs-crossed.svg){width="70%" fig-align="center"}

::: notes
These are the practical traps that turn a good idea into a mis-specified model. The "too few groups" point is the most common: with a handful of patients tau is essentially unestimable and the model can collapse toward complete pooling or misbehave — this is where Bayesian priors on tau genuinely help over lme4. Nested vs crossed is about writing (1 | hospital/patient) versus (1 | batch) + (1 | patient) to match how the units actually relate. The fixed/random choice for treatment trips people up: few, chosen, of-interest levels → fixed. End on the reassurance that unbalanced data is a feature, not a bug, unlike naive averaging.
:::

## Optional: the maths behind random effects {.smaller}

For measurement $j$ in patient $i$:

$$
y_{ij} \;=\; \mu \;+\; b_i \;+\; \varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad
b_i \sim \mathcal N(0,\tau^2),
\quad
\varepsilon_{ij} \sim \mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)
$$

- $\mu$ — overall mean (fixed effect); $b_i$ — patient level (random effect); $\varepsilon_{ij}$ — measurement level.
- $b_i \sim \mathcal N(0,\tau^2)$ is the prior on the patient offsets; the weight $w$ of partial pooling follows from it.
- A flat model treats all $N$ measurements as independent, so its standard error shrinks like $1/\sqrt{N}$; with clustering, $N$ cells are worth only about $N / (1 + (m-1)\,\text{ICC})$ independent samples, for $m$ cells per patient.

::: notes
Optional slide for students who like equations; nothing in the main path depends on it. It is the two-level picture written in symbols: mu + patient offset + measurement noise, each offset drawn from a normal with variance tau^2, each noise term from a normal with variance sigma^2. The last bullet is the formula behind the "effective samples" readout in the pseudoreplication demo: with ICC 0.2 and 20 cells per patient, 120 cells / (1 + 19 x 0.2) = 25.
:::

## Summary {.smaller}

| Concept | Key fact |
|---|---|
| Biological replicate | independent unit; sets your power to generalise |
| Technical replicate | same unit remeasured; reduces measurement noise only |
| Pseudoreplication | counting technical reps as biological → false confidence |
| Complete / no / partial pooling | ignore groups / separate per group / **compromise** |
| Shrinkage | group estimates pulled toward the grand mean, most for small groups |
| Random effect | a patient's offset from the overall mean, drawn from a shared spread $\tau$ |
| Two variances | $\sigma^2$ within, $\tau^2$ between; $\text{ICC}=\tau^2/(\tau^2+\sigma^2)$ |
| Correct uncertainty | error bars reflect number of **groups**, not measurements (demo: 41% vs 6% false alarms) |
| R | `lmer(y ~ x + (1\|group))`; Bayesian `brm(...)` — same formula |
| Bayesian view | a random effect **is** an adaptive prior on group means |

::: notes
The table is the revision sheet. Drill the through-line one more time: data are grouped, groups are not independent draws, so model the grouping; partial pooling gives each group a shrunken estimate and, crucially, gives the whole analysis honest uncertainty tied to the number of independent units. The R syntax (1 | group) is identical in the frequentist lme4 and Bayesian brms worlds. Close on the unifying idea for this block — a hierarchical model is a Bayesian model that learns its own prior for the group parameters — which is why the topic lives here even though the tooling also exists in a frequentist form.
:::
